old_title: Ukraine war live: Explosions rock Kyiv as child among three killed in Russian strikes
new_title: Ukraine war latest: Zelensky warns North Korea could send 50,000 troops to Russia
old_text:
At least three people, including a child, were among those killed in Russian strikes in the region surrounding capital Kyiv in the early hours today, officials said.
The Russian strikes were recorded at three locations in the Boryspil district, near the capital. Three more people were injured in the attack, said Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv military administration.
Fires and powerful explosions that shook the centre of the city were reported in two districts, mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
The attack comes at a time Ukraine is evidently chronically short of air defences capable of downing Russia's ballistic missiles.
Yesterday, a Russian strike hit a football stadium in Odesa, injuring at least one person.
The strike hit the 34,000-seater Chornomorets Stadium. The shelling destroyed the roof, windows, and stands, according to Ukraine's State Emergency Service.
A 29-year-old woman was injured with shrapnel wounds, Odesa's regional governor Oleh Kiper said.
The attack came a day before a Ukrainian Premier League game between Chornomorets and Kolos. No official announcement has been made yet over whether the match will be postponed or cancelled.
Zelensky wants 'concrete results' in developing anti-ballistic missile defence system
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine aims to achieve "concrete results" by the end of this year in developing a European anti-ballistic missile defence system under the Freyja programme.
"Ukraine is capable of producing its missile and launcher, while our partners will provide the necessary components and critical elements - radars, sensors, and everything else required ... Others spent decades developing their systems. Ukraine must do this as quickly as possible, with concrete results already in place by the turn of 2026-2027," he said.
He also said Ukraine is accelerating work on its own ballistic missile programme, adding that tests have shown "strong potential" and that the goal is to turn it into a "real weapon".
"We are creating all the necessary conditions to make that happen."
Ukraine are hitting deep inside Russia - but don't expect Putin to capitulate yet
Russia's war on Ukraine has entered its latest phase, with each side making use of increasing numbers of long-range munitions to strike deep into the other's territory.
In the early summer of this year, there was a surge of optimism across the media when it became clear that Ukraine was stepping up its strikes at enormous ranges into Russia, and there was little that Moscow could do about it. But that optimism needs to be balanced against the new reality that with anti-missile interceptor systems exhausted, there is not much Ukraine itself can do to blunt Russian missile attacks. For now, those attacks sow misery and death by blasting residential areas with little warning: but next winter, they could once again target heating and power infrastructure and have an even more devastating effect on Ukraine's ability to keep its people alive than last year.
Russia's campaign against Ukrainian civilian infrastructure is not new: it began almost as soon as it became clear that Russia had failed in its initial objective of swiftly overrunning the country in February 2022. But its new character today results both from massive increases in the numbers of missiles and drones available to Russia, and the way they have outstripped Ukraine's air defences.
The reluctance of allies to provide the weapons needed to take the fight to Moscow has seen the Ukrainians carry out their own campaign against their enemies' infrastructure - but, Keir Giles writes, we know by now that Russia's leader is happy to let his country burn.
Zelensky arrives in Serbia for first visit
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Serbia on Friday for his first visit to the Balkan country expected to focus on economic cooperation and bids by both countries to secure European Union membership.
Zelensky posted a video on Telegram showing his arrival ahead of talks with populist president Aleksandar Vucic and other officials.
"We will be speaking about expanding economic ties between our countries, relations with the European Union, and other things that can work for our peoples, as well as security issues," Zelensky wrote.
Zelenskiy's visit will likely sour ties between Serbia and Russia, its long-time ally and main natural gas supplier.
On Thursday, Vucic said the two leaders would discuss European Union accession bids as well as economic and energy cooperation.
Watch: Trump brushes off Russia's attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine
Russian attacks kill two in Ukraine's southeastern Dnipropetrovsk Region
Russian strikes on Ukraine's southeastern Dnipropetrovsk Region on Friday killed two people and injured six, the regional governor said.
Oleksandr Hanzha said Russian forces had launched nearly 50 attacks on five districts in the region, deploying drones, artillery and aerial bombs.
Two people were killed near Nikopol, a frequent Russian target on the western bank of the Dnipro River, opposite the Russian-held Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant.
One of the wounded was in a serious condition, Ganzha said.
EU's Von der Leyen welcomes US Senate's backing of Russia energy sanctions
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen welcomed a vote in the US Senate that backed sweeping Russian energy sanctions, advancing a long-delayed measure backed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
"Coming on the back of the EU's 21st package, I welcome the US Senate's adoption of the Graham Bill," wrote von der Leyen on X.
"Together, let us drain Russia's means to continue a war it cannot win. With hard-hitting, complementary sanctions, Europe and the United States can once again show what historic partners can achieve when we act together," added von der Leyen.
Zelensky thanks US Senate for passage of Russia sanctions bill
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky expressed thanks to the US Senate on Friday for the passage of a bill imposing sweeping sanctions on Russia.
"We are very grateful to the US Senate and to everyone who supports Ukraine," Zelensky said on X.
"Adopting the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act certainly helps increase pressure on the aggressor to bring this insane Russian war against our independence and our people to an end," he said.
Russia dismisses German drone incident as 'fabricated provocation'
The Russian embassy in Berlin dismissed a suspected drone attack at a major German air freight hub this week as "fabricated provocation" on Friday, saying it was another example of accusations against Russia without evidence.
"The embassy is expressing its concern about a new wave of anti-Russian hysteria in Germany," said a statement published on its website in German and Russian.
German federal prosecutors launched a probe this week into what they described as a serious attack that could have impacted foreign and domestic security.
"It is obvious that this hastily fabricated provocation only serves the interests of Kyiv and the militarist wing of the European political class," the Russian embassy said in its statement.
Three killed in Russian strikes in Kyiv region
A child is among three killed after Russian forces attacked the region surrounding capital Kyiv on Saturday, an official said.
Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv regional administration, said Russian strikes were recorded at three locations in the Boryspil district, near the capital.
Three more people were injured in the attack, he said.
In the capital itself, fires were reported in two districts, mayor Vitali Klitschko said, following an air raid alert.
Reuters witnesses heard several powerful explosions that shook the centre of the city.
Ukraine is chronically short of air defences capable of downing Russia's ballistic missiles.
new_text:
Volodymyr Zelensky believes that North Korea is preparing to send up to 50,000 troops for deployment in Russia, amid fresh warnings Moscow could order an attack on a Nato country within weeks.
The Ukrainian president told United News on Saturday: "If at first it was about hundreds, then thousands, now it has been decided that from 30 to 50 thousand North Koreans [will go to] the territory of Russia."
He claimed Pyongyang was planning to study the lessons of the war in Ukraine and could present a "threat" to "other states in the Asian direction", urging closer cooperation between Kyiv and South Korea.
Earlier this week it emerged that US intelligence believes that Russian president Vladimir Putin could order an attack on a Nato member within weeks to test the alliance's resolve.
US officials told the Wall Street Journal that the new reports considered the possibility of a small land incursion or cyber attacks across eastern Europe sometime between this autumn and 2029.
The likelihood of the worst case scenario - a cross-border incursion - gets more probably with time, according to the reports. The US has reportedly depleted key missile stockpiles in the war with Iran.
Russia wants 30,000 more North Korean soldiers to fight Ukraine. Is the West at risk?
Soldiers, weapons and now a missile unit have all been deployed by North Korea in a bid to support Russia in its ongoing war against Ukraine.
It marks the country's most significant involvement in a conflict since the 1950s.
In light of recent reports, here's everything we know about the two countries' growing military ties.
What are the latest reports?
According to an official at Ukraine's GUR military intelligence agency, a North Korean missile unit that could be equipped with up to 120 ballistic missiles and six launchers for attacks on Ukraine has begun deploying to western Russia.
The official added that the unit comprises around 90 North Korean personnel and is expected to be based in the Voronezh region of Russia.
Ukraine honours its 'collector of souls' volunteer killed while recovering the war dead
Ukraine paid tribute on Saturday to Oleksiy Yukov, a volunteer who spent more than two decades recovering bodies of civilians and soldiers - many of them Russian - killed by war.
An Orthodox Christian service was held at the Cathedral of Saint Volodymyr, in central Kyiv, where thousands of people gathered to pay their respects following his death in a landmine explosion during a recovery mission on Wednesday.
Mourners also gathered at Kyiv's main Maidan Square, many dropping to their knees as a sign of respect as his casket was brought to the site. Memorial services were also held in other cities.
Yukov, 40, founded the organisation known as Platsdarm, or Bridgehead, because he believed that all the dead deserve a proper burial. He became known as a "collector of souls."
Trump brushes off Russia's attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine
Donald Trump brushed off a question about Russia's attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine, stating that the United States is "separated by an ocean."
The US president was speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Thursday when a journalist said: "Russia seems to have increased their attacks on civilians. That must be of concern to you?"
"We're not involved... We're separated by an ocean," the US president replied. "But I hate to see 25,000 young people a month get killed and that's what's happening between Russia and Ukraine."
"We're working on it and I think we're making progress."
Ukraine's latest strike on Russian Wildberries warehouse shown in satellite images
Kyiv launched another drone strike on a Wildberries warehouse yesterday in Yekaterinburg, Russia, marking the 20th such attack since 18 July as part of a three-week campaign to 'bring the war home' to ordinary Russians.
The latest incident involved three drones hitting the roof of the logistics centre, though the company reported the resulting blaze was contained and most goods remained undamaged.
Satellite imagery from Reuters indicates that these Ukrainian attacks have collectively destroyed one-fifth of the Russian online retailer Wildberries' total storage capacity.
North Korea to send up to 50,000 troops to Russia, says Zelensky
Volodymyr Zelensky says that North Korea is preparing to send 30-50,000 troops to be deployed in allied Russian territory.
Speaking to Ukraine's United News, he says Pyongyang is "studying" the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, and hoping to "gain experience in modern warfare under Russia".
He said: "We have already found North Korean missiles on the territory of Ukraine. Today, this is already an established fact."
Russia says it struck vessels and military facilities supporting Ukraine in Odesa and Mykolaiv
Russia continued strikes on Ukrainian port infrastructure and vessels supporting the Ukrainian military, Russia's defence ministry said on Saturday.
The ministry said Russian forces used precision air-launched weapons and attack drones to hit military warehouses containing communications and electronic warfare equipment in the Black Sea port of Odesa.
In the port of Mykolaiv, Russian forces struck a cargo vessel carrying military equipment and a warehouse storing weapons and military supplies, the ministry said.
It added that another dry cargo vessel transporting military supplies for Ukraine's armed forces was hit in the Black Sea.
Turkey says Russia told that Ukraine should declare moratorium in Black Sea
Turkish foreign minister Hakan Fidan said that Ankara had conveyed to Russia and Ukraine they should declare a moratorium on their attacks in Black Sea.
Speaking to the state-run Anadolu news agency, Fidan said Turkey had conveyed its concerns about attacks on vessels in the Black Sea to both countries and was implementing certain security measures of its own, but did not elaborate further.
A drone likely from Ukraine explodes in Bulgaria near a gas pipeline
A drone entered Bulgarian airspace and exploded close to an international gas pipeline shortly after crossing the border from Romania.
There were no casualties or damage.
The defence ministry in Sofia, Bulgaria's capital, later said there were indications the drone was the kind used by Ukrainian armed forces and that the incident was likely accidental.
Bulgaria and Romania are both members of Nato and the European Union.
A Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesperson said the Ukrainian military was looking into the incident but that it did not deliberately target Bulgaria.
Heorhii Tykhyi said on Saturday that Ukraine and Bulgaria were in "close contact" to establish the circumstances of the incident.
Bulgaria's prime minister Rumen Radev said the drone exploded just after 5am about 100 metres (109 yards) inside Bulgarian territory.
It was not detected or identified while flying through either Romanian or Bulgarian airspace.
German minister warns of daily 'hybrid warfare' after suspected drone attack
Germany faces daily hybrid warfare attacks from abroad, interior minister Alexander Dobrindt was quoted as saying on Sunday, following a suspected attack attempt involving an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
Dobrindt told the newspaper Bild am Sonntag that foreign powers wanted to subdue Germany politically and socially by stirring up fear there.
Dobrindt highlighted the expansion of drone research in Germany as part of the response to the new threats.
"We're not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," Dobrindt said.
"Espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks, or covert operations by foreign powers aimed at destabilising Germany or inflicting direct harm are a constant reality."
The newspaper's advance release of the interview did not say whether he identified any countries in particular.
After the drone loaded with explosives was discovered at the airport in eastern Germany on Tuesday, some German lawmakers pointed the finger at Russia, which has been at war with Ukraine since its military invasion of the country in 2022.
The Russian embassy in Berlin on Friday dismissed the Leipzig event as a "fabricated provocation", saying it was another example of accusations against Russia without evidence.
Hungary faces nuclear plant crisis as Danube river levels remain dangerously low
Hungary's Paks nuclear plant continues to face a "difficult" situation, despite expectations of a temporary rise in Danube river levels following rains in Austria. Prime Minister Peter Magyar conveyed this update via a Facebook video on Friday.
The plant has been operating at approximately 10 per cent of its full capacity since late last week.
